entries.title: The best books on Ecology, recommended by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi
entries.summary: There is romance in the study of ecology, explains the conservationist Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi—whose new book draws from twenty years studying wild snow leopards. Here he recommends five excellent ecology books, from a study of the Serengeti lion to one man's search for a most elusive owl, that get to the heart of what it is to study the natural world. This interview appeared first on Five Boo
entries.content:
You are a scientist and conservationist of many years, and now also the author of a new book on snow leopards, which draws from your 20 years of study in some of the world’s most remote regions. What do you think a good book about ecology should do?

I think a good book about ecology should make the reader curious about nature and arouse a desire in them to step outside and connect with nature in whichever way they can. While the reader learns new things about nature, they should also feel emotionally involved and realise that they are not separate from what is being discussed in the book but rather an integral part of it.

How do you balance the science with storytelling in your own work?

Science does not occur in isolation. The process of doing science has a rich backdrop of evocative stories. Embedding science in these stories also helps ground the work and make it more human. The balance really depends on the style of writing. If the science is esoteric then I like to balance it with deeper stories. If the science is fun then I try humour.

Your first book recommendation is The Serengeti Lion: A Study of Predator-Prey Relations by the eminent field biologist George Schaller, published in 1972. It won the National Book Award in the United States the following year. Would you introduce it to our readers?

The Serengeti Lion was the first book that showed how we can study large wild animals in their natural habitats. This book had a unique appeal for both professionals and amateurs. Now, more than 50 years after its publication, it still remains a very accessible book for people interested in learning about the scientific study of wildlife.

The author, George Schaller, has written many books from different environments ranging from the rainforests of Rwanda to the Tibetan Plateau but this book is the best example of the early years of wildlife biology.

Yes, I’m familiar with Schaller. He’s a major player in Peter Matthiessen’s classic travel book The Snow Leopard; he’s cited in Dian Fossey’s Gorillas in the Mist because he studied the Virunga mountain gorillas before she got there. Just as an aside, he is the subject of a new biography, Homesick for a World Unknown by Mirian Horn.

Schaller was a pioneer who demonstrated how we can study wildlife in their natural habitats and still go beyond descriptions and actually quantify their ecology, behaviour, and deploy this knowledge to further their conservation. But he did not just stop at doing scientific studies, he went on to write a book about each of his research projects and made the work accessible to the world.

Before Schaller, only hunters had tried to meet species like the gorilla and the lion in their natural habitats. He was the first person who ventured in these spaces without a gun. He walked in simply with a notebook, pen, a pair of binoculars and cameras. He stayed in the field for long durations, often several months at a time and multiple years for a single study. Sometimes he moved his entire family to his field sites and they all lived there. In more ways than one he opened the path for the many biologists who followed.

Next you’ve chosen to recommend Owls of the Eastern Ice by the US conservationist Jonathan Slaght, about his work with the Blakiston’s fish owl, in the far-eastern reaches of Russia. I remember this made quite an impact on release in 2020.

Owls are present nearly in every habitat around the world. They are also popular in art and culture. But other than the barn owl, and one or two other species, we know very little about them. Jonathan Slaght uses his excellent writing skills to illuminate a very remote part of the world, the far east of Russia, and an almost unknown species, the Blakiston’s Fish Owl, one of the largest species of owls in the world.

Thanks to this book, I know more about this distant species of owl than some of the other owls that I find in my backyard.

Ecologists seem unusually talented, among scientists, at literary work. Would you agree? Do you think there’s something inherently romantic in the pursuit of the science itself that lends itself so well to the page?

I think, among ecologists, for those with an interest in literature have easy access to interesting material through their work. They work gives that access to travel, diverse cultures, diverse nature, and adventure, which are all essential ingredients for a good story. They also live a life that is very appealing to many but very few actually get to live it and so they have a ready readership. So, yes, there is a romance in the study of ecology that is unmatched in most other sciences.

The Song of the Dodo by David Quammen, your next choice, has appeared several times on our site. The biologist Sean B Carroll described it as “a great hybrid of rich history and contemporary science.” Tell us more.

If I had to pick just one book, it would be The Song of the Dodo. It blends great writing with one of the greatest ecological theories of our time, the theory of ‘island biogeography’, and deploys it to bring attention to one of the greatest challenges of our time, the sixth mass extinction.

It makes you fall in love with literature, then teaching you about the science and then calls the reader to arms to prevent this oncoming tragedy.

That leads us nicely on to No Way Home: The Decline of the World’s Great Animal Migrations by David Wilcove. I suppose this, like the Quammen book, is encouraging us to think of the interdependence of species and ecosystems. What’s his argument?

This work draws our attention to the wonderful natural phenomenon of animal migrations. We have all been awed by the great footages of the wildebeest migrations in the grasslands of Africa. But there are equally incredible migrations by a host of other species including the butterflies, birds, turtles and mammals.

This book highlights some of the most remarkable animal migrations that still exist on our planet. This migrations will disappear well before those species go extinct. I am hopeful that we will be able to save many of these species, but will we be able to prevent these migratory behaviours from going extinct? I am not so sure.

Saving these migrations requires us to protect very large tracts of land and waterscapes which is looking increasing difficult in a rapidly changing world.

And finally, I think that brings us to The Great Soul of Siberia: In Search of the Elusive Siberian Tiger by Sooyong Park. Why do you recommend it?

I find the Siberian tiger to be the greatest enigma after the snow leopard. The ruthlessly difficult landscape and the rarity of the cat makes it very difficult to penetrate this world of this majestic cat. The author demonstrates the great amount of patience and tenacity needed to study this species. He embodies the amazing world of the tiger.

This book is also a reminder of the time where the researcher enters the world of the tiger without depending on modern technology of genetics and camera traps. Through the writing we learn more about the natural history skills of reading the pug marks to understand what the tigers are up to. It shows that old school romance of natural history is still around and healthy.

I like that—the old school romance. In the blurb, the book is described as the result of Park’s ‘obsession’ with the tiger. Actually, this is a framing that we often see in ecology books, and it could be applied to your own book and work, too, I think. Is that how it feels from the inside? A scientific survey or study that is also the expression of a fixation or monomania?

Fixation? Yes. Monomania? No.

I think these types of research projects will not happen without a bit of fixations. They are difficult, come at a huge personal cost and the rewards are not significant. We often only see the tip of the iceberg; a lot of the price is paid up front and risks are taken.

Sometimes the risks pay off, but most of the time they don’t. So in some regards there are a lot of overlaps between explorers, mountaineer, and ecologists.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

July 28, 2026

entries.content:
In 1974, British politician Jeffrey Archer lost all his money in a con. As he tried to dig himself out of the financial hole, he wrote his first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, about four men who fall victim to a stock market scam and take revenge on the con man behind it. The novel has never been out of print since its publication. As it celebrates its 50th anniversary, the bestselling author chooses his favourite books about heists and con artists, both fictional and all too real.

50th Anniversary Edition out August 27

Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less by Jeffrey Archer

In 1974, I invested in what I was assured was a wonderful opportunity, an exciting Canadian venture called Aquablast, presented to me by a vice president at the Bank of Boston. It turned out to be a catastrophe for all of us who invested in it. I lost my home, I stood down from Parliament, and my wife Mary took a teaching post in Cambridge so we could keep a roof over our heads.

There are few sensations quite like realising you have been taken in. Your first reaction is disbelief. Then, if you are honest with yourself, embarrassment. And finally the anger, white-hot and sleepless, because you begin to understand that the swindler is not merely taking your money. He is taking your dignity.

Out of that anger came Harvey Metcalfe, the villain of my first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, and the four men who decided to take back what was stolen from them. Not a penny more, and not a penny less. That line has always sounded to me like both a promise and a threat.

Fifty years on, I find the con artist has never gone out of fashion. If anything, the breed has evolved. The swindler in a sharp suit has been joined by the tech founder with a blood-testing machine that doesn’t work, and the financier whose Ponzi scheme swallowed the savings of his own friends.

I have chosen five books here, and I should tell you at once that the hard part was stopping at five. Some are about con artists. Some are about heists. The difference matters. The con artist lives by deception; he talks his way into your wallet and your trust. The heist man lives by craft, by preparation and timing and nerve. What the five have in common is that every one of them found a new way in, and every one of them taught me something I later used.

Goldfinger (1959) by Ian Fleming

When I was a young man, just before I went up to Oxford, I was in a store in Lymington in Hampshire, and I saw this book for sixpence, second-hand, called Goldfinger. That was my first introduction to Ian Fleming. Wow, did I love it. I loved his hero. I loved his villains. Auric Goldfinger was absolutely wonderful, and Oddjob was the worst, wasn’t he? You were just fascinated by him. Ian Fleming was a great storyteller and genuinely original.

The plot turns on robbing the gold reserve at Fort Knox. It’s so big, so impossible, so American, that for years afterwards every thriller writer tried to copy the scale and not one quite managed. The film made the rest of the world fall in love with it. The book got there first.

I was seventeen at the time. Bond has survived. Here we are nearly seventy years later, and they are still discussing who will be the new Bond. That’s what I call surviving.

“The Million Pound Bank-Note” (1893) by Mark Twain

“The Million Pound Bank-Note” is a wonderful story. Two wicked old men have a bet that they produce a million-pound note with the approval of the Bank of England, and they find a very bright man who’s out of work. They give him the million-pound note. Sounds wonderful, until he tries to spend it. But of course he can’t. And he gets himself into a lot of trouble, a lot of debt, and falls in love before the two men return. It’s great fun from beginning to end.

Mark Twain is, of course, a genius. His short stories are probably better than his novels, and his quips are probably even better than his short stories. His wonderful comment about how “when I was a boy of 14, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be 21, I was astonished by how much he’d learned in seven years” is just brilliant.

Another reason for choosing this short story is personal. The premise, that the appearance of wealth functions exactly as wealth itself, is a lesson I had occasion to learn the hard way in 1974, when a vice-president at the Bank of Boston walked into my life with a confident manner and a story about a company called Aquablast. I believed him. I performed almost no due diligence. He took me for everything I had. The Twain short story turned out to be, in a sense, my own story. The only difference is that out of the wreckage Twain wrote a charming entertainment, and out of mine I wrote Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less.

Bad Blood (2018) by John Carreyrou

Bad Blood is the book you hand to anyone who tells you ‘Surely someone would have spotted it?’ Elizabeth Holmes convinced some of the most powerful people in America that she had invented a machine that could run hundreds of medical tests from a single drop of blood. She hadn’t. The machine didn’t work. And by the time the truth emerged, she had raised nearly a billion dollars.

The people Holmes conned were clever financiers with brilliant careers behind them, who nine times out of ten would have spotted a con man a hundred yards away. They were titans of the American establishment. They still did not see it. The figures involved, hundreds of millions raised on a machine that did not work, are, as I said in 1974 when the Aquablast scale hit me, staggering. Absolutely staggering.

Theranos’s board, at the peak of the deception, included Henry Kissinger and George Shultz. I met Kissinger once. I found him formal, cautious, clearly brilliant. He made a statement that has stayed with me ever since, and that I now find has taken on a peculiar relevance to the Theranos story. ‘If I go to my grave having been fifty-one per cent right, I’ll be very pleased with myself.’ Holmes, of course, was not fifty-one per cent right. She was almost entirely wrong. Kissinger’s modesty about his own judgment is a useful corrective, especially when the room is full of people who are sure.

Carreyrou’s reporting is meticulous and devastating. Read it for the mechanics of the con. Read it for the warning. Read it, most of all, because the scale of belief a charismatic founder can generate is a pattern that did not die with Theranos. And if it feels at all familiar to a Canadian investment a young Member of Parliament made in 1974, the fault is not entirely mine.

Catch Me If You Can (1980) by Frank Abagnale

This book, the true story of a teenager who impersonated a pilot, a doctor, and a lawyer, and cashed millions in fraudulent cheques before the FBI caught up with him, is so outrageous that it reads like fiction.

What fascinates me about Abagnale himself is the sheer nerve. He had no team. He had no technology. What he had was charm and confidence and the understanding, which every great con artist shares, that people see what they expect to see. If you dress like a pilot and walk like a pilot, nobody asks for your licence.

I love the idea, though I confess a cold fear. Pretty bloody frightening, becoming a pilot and taking me to wherever. Read the book for the audacity. Then read the list of jobs the FBI hired Abagnale for afterwards. It is a surprisingly redemptive end to a con artist’s story, and a reminder that the best con artists and the best detectives often have more in common than either of them will admit.

What we have reached, with modern books and modern films, is a stage where the public wants the bad guy to win. It becomes almost farcical. Catch Me If You Can is the perfect example. Leonardo DiCaprio plays Frank Abagnale, and you want him to win, despite the fact that Tom Hanks, who plays the FBI agent chasing him, is one of the nicest people on earth. That is his problem. He is one of the nicest people on earth. So you want the wicked DiCaprio to win. And actually that is what makes the film. If you wanted him to lose, and didn’t like him, it wouldn’t work. You have to go for it.

The Taking of Pelham 123 (1973) by John Godey

John Godey published the novel in 1973 and Joseph Sargent filmed it the following year with Walter Matthau. What I like about Pelham 123 is that the train is always moving. You feel the tension of movement and action. You realise that Transit Police Lieutenant Zachary Garber—played brilliantly by Walter Matthau in the movie—is the good guy, and he is trying to solve the problem.

What fascinated me was how many angles it was written from. You read it from someone on the platform. You read it from someone in the train. But most of all, in the movie, I enjoyed seeing it from the headquarters, where the work is being done on different television screens. And while they are impotent at one level, because all they can do is press buttons and watch, it didn’t take away from the tension. It added to it. And that is crossed with the obvious puzzle – how are the hijackers, led by Mr Blue, going to escape when they are on a public train in a tunnel? It makes for a very, very exciting denouement, where you discover the bad guy isn’t quite as bad as you thought.

Look at the five books I’ve chosen together and you will notice something. In four of them you find yourself on the side of the criminal. You want Bond’s adversary to be interesting. You want DiCaprio to get away with it. You want the man with the million-pound note to spend it. You want the bad guys—Mr Blue and friends—on that train to turn out better than you feared.

When it comes to bad guys, the truth is the public likes them more than the good guys. They love reading about them. Harvey Metcalfe, who has robbed those four nice young men of their money, is the one everybody wants to follow. Of course they want to see him beaten in the end. But he is who they are following.

Some years after Not a Penny More came out, Pierce Brosnan rang me. He said, ‘I want to play Metcalfe.’ He didn’t want to play the hero. He wanted to play the villain. I think villains are often much more fun to play, to perform, than nice, sweet, delightful, good human beings.

Then there is Bad Blood, and nobody wants Elizabeth Holmes to win. That is the difference between a con on the page and a con in the world, and it is the reason I have never quite been able to enjoy the genre without remembering 1974. The contrast between the elegance of these five books and the ugliness of the reality I encountered is, in the end, why I wrote Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less. When you have been on the wrong end of a con, you don’t want style. You want justice.

Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, the 50th Anniversary Edition, is published on 27 August 2026 by Pan Macmillan and St. Martin’s Press.

July 25, 2026

entries.content:
Henry David Thoreau insisted that "in wildness is the preservation of the world." His words have inspired conservationists to bring many of the planet's more ruggedly beautiful places under environmental protection. But 'wilderness' as a concept has become increasingly contested in recent years, explains Five Books deputy editor Cal Flyn, whose new book The Savage Landscape unravels the history of an electrifying idea.

NEW RELEASE

The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness by Cal Flyn

Thank you for recommending these five books on wilderness. Perhaps you could start us off by talking about what defines a wilderness.

Well, it’s a surprisingly fraught question. I think it’s best for me to say that there are a couple of different ways of defining what a wilderness is, one based primarily on subjective qualities—perceived wildness, fearfulness, remoteness—and the policymaker’s or cartographer’s definition, which is derived according to more objective measures, like distance from roads and the built environment, and which is used to plot maps or define protected areas.

I have always loved and sought out the feeling of entering a wilderness—which to me is tied up with physical challenge, adventure, a sense of exploration and self-sufficiency, as well as a broader sense of coming into direct contact with nature.

To many people, the wilderness is somewhere they seek solitude and the sublime, and where they might strip life back to its essentials. To conservationists, wilderness might be specifically primary or unfelled forest, unploughed ground, an unaltered landscape. But it’s a contested term, because it is not widely agreed what ‘altered’ means, exactly, and it is one that many environmental groups have moved away from using in recent years, because indigenous residents of the wildernesses often argue that the label erases the long human occupation of their homelands.

When I think of wilderness, I think of wild woods, thorny deserts, vast open plains. Is that not right?

It is and it isn’t. These are all landscapes commonly claimed to be wildernesses. The controversy tends to arise around the acceptable level of human impact. In the 1960s, the United States introduced the Wilderness Act, which defined wilderness land as

an area where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain.

It’s rather lyrical for a legal definition, and this framing of wilderness has been extremely influential—not only in America but throughout the global conservation movement. But of course it does conveniently gloss over the long Native American habitation of and management of lands officially designated as wilderness.

The idea that man should be “a visitor who does not remain” has underpinned many inhumane environmental policies, laws that have demanded indigenous groups be forcibly removed from protected areas around the world. This is a big issue in the Congo Basin today, for example; in Uganda, I met dozens of Batwa people who have lived in refugee camps for decades, following their forced eviction from the Virunga national parks. Previously they had lived alongside the Virunga’s famous mountain gorillas for an estimated ten thousand years. More recently, the Baka forest people of Cameroon, the Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic have also been extremely badly treated.

Depending on how you define it, there are an estimated ten million ‘conservation refugees’ like them in the world today—people who have been displaced by the creation of environmentally protected areas, based on this sense that wildernesses should not be populated.

It is a really thorny question. Because if you accept the presence of humans and all environments being human impacted—if you accept that there is no pristine ‘before’ to return to—then one must ask: what exactly is it that we are trying to save? The hard problem of wilderness forces us to interrogate many of conservation’s basic assumptions and overarching objectives.

While researching my book The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness, I travelled all around the world following threads of the story of wilderness, starting from its ancient spiritual roots as a site of epiphany or revelation, and moving through various interpretations of the idea by way of aesthetics, landscape ethics and conservation. The book told through a series of ten journeys to some of the world’s most isolated locations—from the Sinai Desert to the high Himalaya, from the Amazon rainforest to the Antarctic peninsula.

Right. I began my own investigation into the history of wilderness in the deserts of Egypt, examining the desert as a site of revelation in the Abrahamic religions and the later development of Christian asceticism.

Actually, the wilderness appears in many other world religions too: as a place where one might find enlightenment or epiphany through trial. It doesn’t have to be desert—Gautama Buddha abandoned the royal court, including his wife and child, for “remote jungle thickets” and the Hindu prince Rama also journeyed through a “jungle of punishment” dense with shapeshifting demons. Other religions or spiritual movements use wilderness trials as a form of purification: a washing-clean of the mind of daily concerns, preparing it for grander concerns.

The ‘Desert Fathers’ of this book were a loose conglomeration of early Christian ascetics living in the Egyptian deserts, from the third century onwards. Their pared-back approach to worship—abandoning theological texts in favour of direct revelation—and extreme living conditions would trickle down to influence the monastic traditions of both the eastern and western arms of the Church. You can see their direct influence on forest hermits of mainland Europe and Russia, for example, and the cave and mountain hermits of the Levant, and m0re indirectly the Irish missionaries who flung themselves into the ocean in coracles.

Some of the wisdom of those earliest desert ascetics was collected together over many years as the Apophthegmata Patrum, or the ‘sayings’ of the Fathers. The sayings—which often take the form of weird, fable-like stories set in eerie, dusty expanses haunted by demons—are cryptic, sometimes comic, and always intriguing. It’s a book for dipping into, a bit like certain poetry collections. I need to be in the right frame of mind to appreciate them, but sometimes their effect is profound and destabilising.

If you want to know more, I also recommend the writing of John Wortley, especially his Introduction to the Desert Fathers published by Cambridge University Press. There’s also a great book by Peter France called Hermits: The Insights of Solitude that offers a broader sweep through time.

Next you’ve chosen a 1998 collection called The Great New Wilderness Debate, edited by J. Baird Callicott and Michael P. Nelson.

I found this book completely invaluable during my research. Basically it’s a kind of wilderness ‘reader’: a collection of key texts that will help you get your head around the evolution of wilderness into its modern-day iteration as a legal designation and form of environmentally protected area.

There’s lots and lots to read in this book. My copy is almost 700 pages long, and there’s a follow-up collection with the same editors called The Wilderness Debate Rages On if you want more of the same. These also aren’t the kind of books to sit down and read from cover to cover, but rather to pick out the sections that are of special interest to you.

It has extracts of writing by Ralph Waldo Emerson, John Muir and Theodore Roosevelt, for example, that give a sense of developing American thought on wilderness preservation around the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th century. Then it devotes a lot of space to the later deconstruction of the wilderness concept by key thinkers like William Cronon, whose landmark essay ‘The Trouble With Wilderness‘ is reprinted in full. Cronon famously argued that

Far from being the one place on earth that stands apart from humanity, it is quite profoundly a human creation

What he’s arguing, essentially, that wilderness is a construct, an ideal that we project upon the world, “a reflection of our own unexamined longings and desires.” Many of the locations most celebrated for their wilderness qualities, in the US and elsewhere, have actually been purposefully depopulated:

The removal of Indians to create an “uninhabited wilderness”—uninhabited as never before in the human history of the place—reminds us just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is.

I remember reading this essay for the first time and having a kind of dropping sensation, a sense of my entire conception of nature and landscape shifting. It helped me understand that the way I view nature is highly shaped and coloured by my cultural background.

But then there’s a very rousing defence of wilderness as something precious to protect by the activist Dave Foreman, and international input from Ramachandra Guha and Arne Naess. Plus some early discussion of how the wilderness preservation and indigenous rights movements might work together, or not—something that is coming more to the fore in the present.

Those with an academic interest in the subject should definitely also read Mapping Wilderness, edited by Stephen J. Carver and Steffan Fritz, which is more recent. I think it was published in 2016. They are less focused on philosophy and ethics and more focused on generating maps that can be of use to policymakers seeking to designate new nature reserves. It’s a different take and a very practical one. Plus it has global scope.

Right. Because many of the thinkers you’ve mentioned are American, and your third book recommendation looks specifically at the United States wilderness tradition. This is Wilderness and the American Mind by Roderick Nash.

Wilderness was a great preoccupation of American thought all through the 20th century, and Roderick Nash’s book—a pioneering work of environmental history first published in the 1960s, but reprinted and updated several times since then—is a useful key to understanding why. It analyses how ‘wild’ landscapes came to be prized by a colonial society seeking its own monuments in the absence of Roman ruins or established art museums. European settler society either defined itself against Native American culture or simply ignored it, and the westward-sweeping frontier became an important element in the story colonial America told itself about itself—as did the frighteningly alien landscapes the colonists encountered, explored and mapped over the decades.

Anyway, the Nash book is a highly readable work of cultural and environmental history, and the latest edition includes extra content by Nash responding to critiques of his work and new research. It’s a must-read on the topic, especially for Americans but really for everyone with an interest in wilderness preservation and its origins as a movement.

Next you’ve selected Apsley Cherry-Garrard’s The Worst Journey in the World, a first-hand account of Captain Scott’s 1911-1912 expedition to Antarctica. The writers Sara Wheeler and Paul Theroux have both previously recommended it to us; Wheeler described it as “possibly the best book ever written.”

I love that. Academic discussion of wilderness is all very well—and necessary, truly—but I also wanted this list to reflect the savage, unconstrained beauty of the world’s wildest places, especially Antarctica.

If anywhere on Earth really can make a claim to being a true wilderness, it is Antarctica, which was not confirmed to exist until well into the 19th century (although, as qualifier, there is some suggestion from oral history it may have been encountered by Māori navigators centuries earlier, although this is difficult to substantiate). Though already impacted by climate change, large swathes of Antarctica have literally never been set foot upon, unlike almost everywhere else on Earth. It and the deep sea are the closest things we have to truly ‘pristine’ environments.

Cherry-Garrard’s account of his time in Antarctica capture the beauty and the horror of the polar south. He was not among the party that made the infamous and ill-fated expedition to the South Pole, but he did take part in an extremely gruelling journey through the polar winter to gather emperor penguin eggs for scientific purposes, during which the men lost their tent to a snowstorm and only barely survived. Cherry-Garrard’s teeth broke apart in his gums due to the violence with which they were chattering.

Horrible.

The conditions these men faced were truly extreme, and they were working out how to do it as they went. It’s a classic wilderness narrative. I love to read diaries of explorers—they are invariably pushed to their physical and psychological limits. Often they, like Cherry-Garrard, are beautiful writers, or, at the very least, recording strange and beautiful natural phenomena, which can be utterly bewitching to encounter through prose.

Sara Wheeler herself wrote a great biography of Cherry-Garrard. That’s worth mentioning too. As is Francis Spufford’s cultural history I May Be Some Time, a sort of Anglo-Antarctic equivalent to what Roderick Nash did for American wilderness. Spufford digs into what it was, exactly, about Antarctica that so caught the English imagination, and what the ice and the pursuit of the South Pole came to symbolise to the society of the day.

I think that brings us to your final book recommendation, which is Rebecca Solnit’s A Field Guide to Getting Lost. Why do you recommend it in this context?

I love this book. Actually, I love all the books by Solnit that I’ve read, but I have a special soft spot for A Field Guide to Getting Lost. It is a slim, essayistic book about losing objects, losing one’s way, losing oneself, and the art—as she puts it—“of being at home in the unknown.” Early on, she quotes the frontiersman Daniel Boone:

I never was lost in the woods in my whole life, though I was once confused for three days.

I think that gets to the heart of it very well.

I’ve spent years now trying to get my head around the pull of the wilderness and how to find it. I’ve realised that the harder I pursue it, the harder I try to pin it to the map, the further it seems to slip from my grip. Wherever I went, no matter how far I travelled, the wilderness was always reported to me to be just over the next rise, around the next bend.

What I’m really looking for when I’m looking for wilderness is that sense of being in uncharted territory, off the map. Lost, or, at the very least, confused in the way Daniel Boone relates. Of course one can experience that on an Antarctic expedition, or on a ship on the open sea, or after many days or weeks on the trail. But the demands of that kind of adventure travel can be intense, and may keep you trapped in a highly logistical, rational, practical mindset—constantly calculating mileage or pack weight or altitude gain. Carrying a mobile phone or a satellite emergency beacon is useful and necessary, but it also eats into that mental freedom, the sense of being cast-adrift, which is the reason you have gone there in the first place.

Getting lost or surrendering oneself in the way Solnit is talking about can be achieved much closer to home. The poet Gary Snyder once wrote:

A person with a clear heart and open mind can experience the wilderness anywhere on earth. It is a quality of one’s own consciousness.

I’ve come to see that the argument about wilderness legislation and land designation is an attempt to answer a different kind of question. An important one—one tied up in the future health of our planet—but one bound up in physical realities. The wilderness may yet be confirmed to be a physical place, but it has certainly always been a metaphysical one. And, as such, it has been an object of fascination for millennia.
